no-progressive-party-candidate.summary: With Roosevelt out of the race, candidates outside the two parties take 8.1% of the vote, against 35.0% in 1912, and the two-party split moves 5.2 points toward Wilson. California, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and 4 more flip, but Wilson still wins, 531–0. Taft wins in 0 of 100 draws. Extremely low confidence. The interviews point the other way from the historical record.
assumptions: Voters who chose the third-party candidate in 1912 redistribute to the two major nominees or abstain, according to their prior leanings and the issues they cared about.
howIGotThis: What changed: The former President's new party of progressive insurgents fields no presidential candidate, and the third candidate is off the ballot.

What historians found (11 findings, strong evidence): No direct estimate exists for a 1912 vote without Roosevelt's party. Leads suggest Progressive voters would split, with many going to Wilson and Republicans in the Midwest staying with Taft. The 1924 La Follette run is an analogue with different coalitions. No numeric transfer estimates were found.
The numbers: the 1910 and 1920 census counts interpolated to 1912 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1912 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.
Extremely low confidence: The interviews point the other way from the historical record.

findings.claim: Roosevelt and other Progressive candidates clearly shaped the 1912 outcome, including an unusually large Democratic class in the 63rd Congress. Vote-transfer estimates were not retrieved.
Progressives within the Democratic Party stayed united behind Wilson. Many Ohio Republicans backed Roosevelt for the Republican nomination but would not follow him into the new party.

before.quote: The protective tariff keeps our wages up and our shops steady. I'll stick with the administration's man, though I'll grant the other fellow makes sense on some matters.
before.reason: Fred Ellis is a white native-born male of voting age in Michigan with a settled household engaged in store or office work, making him eligible and likely to vote. His reading on the tariff and local option issues, combined with his stake in business stability and protective duties for wage-earners, suggests lean toward the incumbent administration's candidate, though he shows some openness to the progressive insurgent alternative.

after.quote: These big trusts have squeezed working men long enough. The fellow from the other party means to cut them down to size and bring prices back where they ought to be.
after.reason: Fred Ellis is a Michigan tradesman in a town, eligible to vote in 1912. The anti-monopoly and tariff-cutting platform of Wilson appeals to working men concerned about trusts and the cost of living, issues much discussed in recent newspapers he has likely encountered. His choice leans toward Wilson but remains somewhat uncertain given the appeal of F's court authority and tariff protections for American wages.

before.quote: The big trusts have gotten too powerful, squeezing out smaller concerns and keeping working men's wages down. That former President understands what needs fixing.
before.reason: Reed is a mill or railroad worker in Massachusetts who has read recent reform advocacy focused on child labor, women's wages, and trust regulation. He can pass the literacy test. The brief shows him exposed to progressive critiques of concentrated wealth and inadequate protections for workers, which align most closely with the insurgent platform.

after.quote: These trusts have gotten too powerful, squeezing out the small man. The Democrat's talk of criminal penalties and stopping those holding companies makes more sense to me than the Republican way.
after.reason: Ernest Reed, a mill or shop worker in Massachusetts, has access to recent newspaper coverage of campaign positions on trusts, child labor, wages, and banking reform. His economic circumstances and the issues emphasized in what he has read point toward the Democratic nominee, though some uncertainty remains about tariff impacts on industrial employment.

before.quote: I can't vote myself, but my husband will be voting tomorrow. I hope he makes a good choice for all of us.
before.reason: Helen Dawson is a woman living in Indiana in 1912, and women cannot vote for president in Indiana. She is therefore legally barred from casting a presidential ballot regardless of her preferences or intent.

before.quote: I'd like to have a say in things, but the law doesn't allow us women to vote. My husband will cast the ballot for our household.

after.quote: I'd vote if I could, but women don't have that right here. My husband will have to make the choice for our household.

before.quote: The trusts bleed us dry while the politicians in the other parties do nothing about it. This man Wilson seems to want to cut the tariffs on what we need and go after the monopolies proper.
before.reason: Thomas Carter works in a mill for wages and would be drawn to Wilson's commitment to tariff cuts on necessities and goods competing with trusts, which would lower his cost of living. The recent newspaper accounts of Hill's votes against income tax reform trouble him, and Wilson explicitly opposes corporate campaign contributions and favors antitrust enforcement, appealing to a wage-earner's suspicion of monopoly power.

after.quote: The trusts have had their way long enough. A man working for wages needs cheaper goods and honest competition, not protected monopolies.
after.reason: Thomas Carter is a mill worker in Massachusetts whose household depends on wages from industrial labor. He would favor tariff cuts that lower prices on necessities and goods competing with trusts, and would support aggressive antitrust enforcement. Wilson's platform on these issues aligns with his economic interests as a working man.

before.quote: The Republican's kept tariffs high to protect our goods and our wages, and they've gone after the big trusts too. That's what matters to a man trying to make a living from the land.
before.reason: James Hayes is a Texas farmer who can vote if he pays the poll tax, which his household's farming income likely allows. The tariff and currency issues dominating the recent news directly affect agricultural prices and credit availability, making him attentive to the election, though his choice reflects uncertainty about which party best serves rural interests.

after.quote: I reckon I'll likely get into town tomorrow to vote. The Republican's been good for business, I'd say, though times are hard for all of us farmers.
after.reason: Hayes is a Texas farmer who can pay the poll tax and is eligible to vote. The brief mentions currency and tariff debates but provides no specific information about Hayes's personal economic views, party loyalty, or voting intentions, leaving considerable uncertainty about whether he will vote and for whom.

before.quote: I can't vote—women don't have the right in Illinois. My husband will go to the polls tomorrow, but that's all I can do.
before.reason: Emma Brown is a woman living in Illinois in 1912, and women cannot vote for president in Illinois. Legal disenfranchisement makes it impossible for her to cast a ballot regardless of her preferences.

after.quote: I can't vote—women aren't allowed to in Illinois. My husband will have to decide for us both tomorrow.
after.reason: Emma Brown is a woman living in Illinois in 1912, and women are legally barred from voting for president in this state. Her inability to vote is a matter of settled law, not circumstance.

before.quote: These trusts and tariffs keep squeezing us working folks. The man standing for free trade and breaking up the big combines makes the most sense for my family's pocketbook.
before.reason: Harry Tate works for wages in an Illinois mill or railroad. The newspaper articles he has read in recent weeks criticize high protective tariffs and trusts as causing the cost of living to rise for working people, while praising the income tax as a check on wealth concentration. Wilson's platform of cutting tariffs immediately and enforcing antitrust law directly addresses these concerns closest to Tate's economic interests and the populist sentiment evident in the local press he reads.

after.quote: The trusts and tariffs have squeezed us long enough. That fellow Wilson says he'll cut the duties and go after them hard. Time to give him a chance.
after.reason: Harry Tate works for mill or railroad wages in Illinois and has read local criticism of high tariffs and trusts harming working people. Wilson's platform on tariff reduction, antitrust enforcement, and opposition to corporate influence aligns with these concerns that dominate his recent reading.

before.quote: The trusts and the speculators are taking all the profit from our work. That man from the other party wants to cut out the middlemen and let us farmers get a fair shake at last.
before.reason: Arthur Green is a rural Virginia farmer struggling with the high cost of living and low farm profits described in recent agricultural reporting. The Democratic nominee's emphasis on revenue-only tariffs and immediate cuts to duties protecting trusts aligns with his economic self-interest, while his party's strength in the House suggests practical power to enact farm relief.

after.quote: The trusts have their boot on the farmer's neck, and somebody needs to cut them loose. That man talks about doing it proper, through the law.
after.reason: Arthur Green, a Virginia farmer struggling with low margins and high costs, has read repeatedly about rural credit reform and corporate overreach. Wilson's platform of tariff cuts on necessities, aggressive antitrust action, and campaign finance reform aligns with the farmer's material interests and the reform sentiment circulating in agricultural papers he encounters.

before.quote: I can't vote tomorrow, so it doesn't much matter what I think. My husband will cast his ballot.
before.reason: Florence Dawson is a woman in Connecticut in 1912, and women are legally barred from voting for president in this state. She cannot cast a ballot regardless of her preferences.

after.quote: I wish I could vote tomorrow, but women don't have that right here yet, no matter what anyone says.
after.reason: Florence Dawson is a 22-year-old woman living in Connecticut in 1912, and women cannot vote for president in that state or any other state at this time. She is legally barred from casting a ballot.

before.quote: I wish I could vote tomorrow, but the law doesn't allow it. My husband will have to cast our household's ballot.
before.reason: Anna Reed is a woman living in Alabama in 1912, and women are explicitly barred from voting for president in the state. She cannot lawfully cast a ballot.

after.quote: I wish I could have a say in it, but the law won't allow women to vote here, not yet anyway.
after.reason: Anna Reed is a woman living in Alabama in 1912, and women are legally barred from voting for president in the state. No circumstance in the brief suggests she has exceptional legal standing to vote.

reading.summary: Speaker urges ending child labor, a living wage, and one rest day weekly.
North Dakota account of a court blocking a proposal; recall called unsafe.
Editorial says trusts suppress competition yet bring efficiency; all parties blame some for harm.
Union committee proposes abolishing the electoral college and electing Supreme Court judges by vote.
Age-Herald says the currency reform fight will carry into the next Congress.
Bankers divided on currency plan at Detroit; a mayor loses his temper.
Banker says New York banks hold about 40 percent of all currency.
Piece discusses confusion over the terms Money Power and Money Trust.
Praises a candidate's record on labor, primaries, Confederate pensions, and the federal income tax.
Editorial says liquor interests push half-way county option candidates to fool dry voters.
Arkansas recall and bond petitions called dead because only three amendments are allowed.
Bankers' currency commission tells Detroit convention it will wait until after elections.
Article says the rigid currency system will pinch badly next month despite bumper crops.
Party platform report approves ending the highway commission and discusses currency reform.
Discusses state minimum wage boards for women and the risk of interstate undercutting.
Letter argues woman suffrage may not be expedient and could enlarge the illiterate vote.
Retail ad column jokes about the high cost of living and John D. Rockefeller.
Criticizes Rodenberg for voting against the income tax amendment and for high trust prices.
Article says Hill voted against the income tax amendment and opposes taxing the wealthy.
Says Hill voted with Payne to avoid state conventions on the income tax amendment.
Predicts rural cooperative credit will free farmers from trusts and high living costs.
Items include a lost girl found safe and a New York food-cart owner arrested.
